extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, SF/F workshop participants, workshop leaders, and creative-writing instructors
extracted.subtask_description: A peer-critique protocol (originating at the Milford Writers' Workshop) for giving and receiving feedback on short fiction, especially SF/F: author remains silent while timed, turn-based critiques are given, then the author replies. Emphasizes specific craft axes (plot, character, worldbuilding, prose, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Author silence during critique
rubrics_metrics.description: The author of the work being critiqued sits in silence through the full critique round. They may not interrupt, defend, explain, or respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silence forces the author to listen rather than rebut, prevents the workshop from becoming an argument, ensures every critique is heard and absorbed, and reveals what readers actually got from the text without the author's intended meaning interfering. The rule is pedagogical: the text must 'speak for itself' in the absence of the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timed, uninterrupted critique turns
rubrics_metrics.description: Each participant in turn delivers an uninterrupted critique within a strict time limit (typically four minutes, timed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict timing produces high-density feedback in a short time, prevents domination by single speakers, and trains participants to make focused, analytical observations. Anti-patterns: rambling, conversational interruptions, or open discussion during the turn subvert the method's intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's right to reply after critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: After all critiques are delivered, the author has an uninterrupted right to reply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reply is the author's opportunity to ask clarifying questions or respond after having heard all feedback. Guidance implies the reply should not reopen the critique into argumentative back-and-forth but serve to clarify and consider next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story make sense? Is cause-and-effect, sequence, and narrative logic clear and consistent?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for gaps, contradictions, or unclear story mechanics that prevent the reader from understanding what happened and why. A story that fails on plot coherence is considered 'broken' in workshop terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character motivation and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Do characters act believably? Are their motivations, desires, and actions consistent with their characterization?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether actions have credible motivations, whether character choices are justified within the story, and whether behavior remains consistent or intentionally develops. Note where characters function as mere plot devices or act inexplicably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldbuilding internal consistency (esp. in SF/F)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the imagined world internally coherent? Do rules, technologies, cultures, and settings hold together without contradiction?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify places where world rules are violated or underexplained, which can break suspension of disbelief. For SF/F, consistency of speculative elements is a central axis of critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Does interest sustain through the story? Are scenes and narrative beats balanced for momentum and attention?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether early sections drag or later sections rush, whether transitions maintain engagement, and whether the pacing suits the story's scope. Suggest structural edits to redistribute emphasis where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose quality at sentence level
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity, rhythm, and sentence-level infelicities: is the writing clear, economical, and effective?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out unclear sentences, awkward diction, tonal inconsistencies, and rhythmic problems. Examples or brief rewrites can illustrate suggestions. Avoid turning the critique into copyediting-only; connect sentence-level notes to larger story goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre fit / genre conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the work succeed as the kind of story it intends to be? Are genre conventions met or knowingly violated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the story fulfills or deliberately subverts readers' genre expectations and whether those choices are effective. For SF/F, consider whether speculative elements and thematic concerns align with genre norms or purposefully challenge them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of central idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the central idea fresh and productive? Does the concept generate interesting possibilities within the story?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the premise yields new insights or feels derivative. Consider whether the idea is exploited fully and whether its implications are explored rather than merely stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience accessibility / marketability
rubrics_metrics.description: Would this sell? Is the story accessible to its intended audience?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider readership expectations, clarity of concept for potential readers, and commercial prospects. This axis mixes craft assessment with pragmatic publishing considerations; note that marketability judgments can reflect dominant market norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop method encodes craft assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Milford Method itself functions as a craft framework: the methodology shapes what is noticed, valued, and actionable in a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit that workshop procedures are not neutral—they prioritize certain craft axes (e.g., plot, coherence) and thus operate as a rubric. Workshop leaders and participants should recognize these embedded assumptions when applying feedback to diverse texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity and cultural/context sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness that the method privileges Western/Anglophone craft norms and can be hostile to writers using unfamiliar conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarion West's review notes that Milford-style silence can prevent authors from explaining cultural context their work requires. As a criterion for conducting critiques, workshops should allow for cultural framing, avoid enforcing narrow norms, and be cautious about misreading formally unfamiliar storytelling choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favoring critique-confidence over critique-accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: A documented weakness: the method can reward confident-sounding critiques even when they are inaccurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants and leaders should value evidence-based, text-rooted observations and discourage performative certainty. Encourage specificity, citation of passages, and humility in interpretation to improve critique quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique as service to the writer (vs ritual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique should be oriented toward helping the writer improve rather than following ritualized behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that the ritual of timed, public critique can become an end in itself. Alternative, author-centered models emphasize dialogue, framing, and tailoring feedback to the author's goals; consider adopting such practices when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-centered alternatives: framing and dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative models (e.g., CRP / Liz Lerman; Clarion West's moves toward author-centered workshops) allow more dialogue and framing by the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider letting authors provide context, state goals, or flag what kind of feedback they want before critiques begin. These practices can mitigate harms of silence, especially for underrepresented writers, and align critique with the author's intentions and needs.
